utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. Case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We shall continue our proceedings under Rule 15 bis, paragraph A, as Judge Lindholm is still ill. The Prosecution is cross-examining. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Maslic. You said you joined the SDS in 1996. Can you recall when in 1996 you joined the party?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometime in mid-1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And you remain a member of the party?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: The party had been in existence and operating since, I think -- or at least since 1990?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And in that time, you had had an opportunity to consider its policies and indeed observe its policies at work in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And when you joined the party in 1996, obviously you had considered its history, were satisfied with its history, and took the decision to join it?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I thought about it, I didn't really assess the work of the party, but in 1996 I decided, for one simple reason, to get politically involved in one of the political parties that existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Yes, but I assume that you had had an opportunity of seeing its policies at work, were satisfied with those policies, and then joined the party; otherwise, why would you join a party with whose policies you were dissatisfied?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not engaged in politics before 1996 either, and now I'm just an ordinary party member.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Sure. Let me put it to you this way: When you joined the party in 1996, did you violently oppose its policies?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand in what sense you mean this, violently oppose its policies.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: It's a very -- look, all I want to do is put a very simple proposition to you. You joined the party in 1996, you had seen the party at work over the years since 1990; presumably you must have been satisfied with the way it conducted itself and satisfied with its policies and thought that it was the right party for you to join.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that I joined the party in that particular year. I did not think about the history of the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Very well. I'll turn to another topic. Would you agree that whatever the system of exchanges was and however it worked, the result over 1992 and 1993 was that through that system, large numbers of non-Serbs left the municipality of Bosanski Samac and large numbers of Serbs entered the municipality of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: Would Your Honours just bear with me? I want to produce a document -- I see the case manager has just arrived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I want to produce to you a document that appointed you to your position as director of the social welfare centre. Please look at this document and tell me if you recognise it. And if indeed, it is the document whereby you were appointed to the position of director of social welfare.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. And indeed, it's the document that resulted in you being appointed director of social welfare?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, is it an exhibit? MR. DI FAZIO: No. No. I'll produce it. I seek to tender it into evidence. I've got the sufficient number of copies here. May I proceed, or should we wait for the number to be given?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we have the number, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit P160 and ter for the B/C/S. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Now, obviously, it's clear from the document, and of course just the facts in this case, that you were working for the Bosanski Samac Serbian municipality, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: This was a new municipality that had been created for Serb people; correct?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that this municipality had been created for Serbs only. This is a municipality where others lived as well, that is to say, citizens of other ethnic backgrounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: It was a municipality whose political representatives was restricted to members of the SDS and other deputies of Serb nationality, wasn't it? If you wish, I can show you the gazette and the Statute and so on. I prefer not to do that, and so we can move on. But would you agree to that extent, that it was a Serbian municipality?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, really, I think that if this is the line of questioning that is desired, then I think that it is fair to show the witness the documents that have to do with the functioning of the authorities in the municipality of Samac. MR. DI FAZIO: It's not the main topic that I'm interested in. I'd prefer not to embark on this road. It was a simple question. I thought I'd get a certain answer. I got another answer. And I had to ask the question the followed. But it's not the primary topic that I'm interested in. In fact, I'll withdraw -- I won't go down this road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: That's what I was about to say. Withdraw the question. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: It's clear from the document P160 that you have to perform your duties as director pursuant to the law of this new Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That is so, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these are laws that were in force before the war broke out in the territory of the municipality. Those are the laws on child care and social welfare, family-related laws, and all other regulations that were in force. This was the legislation that was borne in mind and these were the laws that we implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Yes. And indeed, any other laws that the municipality might implement which affected your work, you would have to obey them and carry on your work pursuant to those laws; right?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the municipality could not pass laws, only decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You were going to carry out your duties then as director of the social welfare centre of Bosanski Samac, in accordance with the decisions of the civilian authorities in the Serbian municipality of Bosanski Samac. That is correct, at least, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you would agree, wouldn't you, that for an agency conducting important humanitarian work, in those particular circumstances, it was important for you and your agency and the Red Cross to follow the policies and the leadership of the government of the Republika Srpska, first the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and later the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We in this particular institution, first and foremost, pursued the laws that were relevant in that area. These laws and decisions were based on the basic principles of humaneness and giving assistance to people. All these laws and decisions that we applied were nondiscriminatory. They did not discriminate against a single people or ethnic group who lived in the territory of the municipality of Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: No. That -- I understand what you're saying, but in those particular times, it was important -- times of war, the emergence of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, it was important for you and the municipality to follow policies and the leadership of the government; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that I was not involved in politics. I did not come to head the centre as a political appointee. I came first and foremost as a professional in that area. I followed the laws that were in force, not politics.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I'm informed that the LiveNote is not functioning at all for the Prosecution, at least. I don't know if the Defence have similar problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: Oh, I see. And indeed, if we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Since the monitors are functioning, we shall proceed. They will fix the laptops during the break. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And did the Red Cross, the local Red Cross, adhere to the overall policies of the government of the Republika Srpska or the Serbian Republic, particularly where it affected humanitarian issues?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The local Red Cross also applied the basic principles of humaneness and the principles of humanism. As an organisation of humanitarian nature, they did not receive any instructions in terms of the policy pursued by any government. They only had their own tasks that they were supposed to carry out within the legislation that existed in that area. MR. DI FAZIO: Can the witness be shown P5? Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You were -- as director of the social welfare centre and through your involvement with the Red Cross, you were -- MR. DI FAZIO: Could you just -- Mr. Usher, could you just hold the document for the time being?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: As director of the social welfare centre and through your involvement in the Red Cross, you were committed, weren't you, to following humanitarian principles and seeing that humanitarian policy was carried out through your agency and the Red Cross, through your social welfare centre and through the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've already said who the persons who worked there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And you found no impediment to doing that from republican-level government, from the policies of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and later the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: Can you now look at P5. If Your Honours please, I do apologise. May I just briefly look at the document for a good reason. We haven't got our copy here and I just want to very quickly refresh my memory. Perhaps if I might borrow the Court's English copy. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I be of assistance? In the B/C/S version, it is on page 2 of this Official Gazette. So perhaps it would be useful to look at that page. Perhaps the witness can be told to look at the second page, then. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. I'm grateful to my learned friend. I had forgotten that the English is just one extract and I'm grateful for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And I also believe, Witness, that you'll find it under paragraph 386. Now, have you seen this before?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never seen this decision before.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Are you aware of it?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Very well. If you look at paragraph 1, establishing -- the establishment of state borders separating the Serbian people from the other two ethnic communities, you presumably, then, would not know how that was to be effected, carried out.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that I'd never seen this decision and that I'm not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't know if this line of questioning can be pursued now, when the witness doesn't know anything about this decision. It is now really up to the Trial Chamber to see -- to decide whether this decision can be discussed and whether he can actually answer questions that have anything to do with it. He was not a member of parliament or anything, nor was he involved in government in any other way. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, I realise that the witness can no longer tell us anything about the document. He said that he doesn't know anything about it, and that's fine. The document can be taken from him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: One question, though, I have, Mr. Di Fazio, and maybe I could pose it directly to Mr. Maslic. Clearly, you hadn't seen the document, so you can't comment on the document. But in terms of the substance of what was in there, did you know at the time anything concerning the establishment of state borders separating the Serbian people from the other two ethnic communities, separate and apart from the decision itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've already said that I was not involved in politics. I was not involved in government in any way. I was engaged in humanitarian work only in the institution where I was employed. And as for any kind of interpretation of this kind of decision or any opinion, I cannot really go into that because I was not involved in that kind of thing, nor did I give it any thought. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Just one last thing on the document, if I may. In fact, no. The document can be taken away from the witness. Mr. Maslic, 1992, Serbs and Croats and Muslims lived side by side in the municipality of Bosanski Samac, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: If those people were to be separated, that would cause, would it not, humanitarian concerns?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean when you say "separate." They lived in the same town. What do you mean, "separate"?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I know that they lived in the same town, but if they were to be separated, Serbs to be separated from Croats and Muslims --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You are asking the witness to speculate, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Well, yes. Very well. I'll withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: The end result of the exchanges at the end of 1993 was that Bosanski Samac had become a predominantly Serbian-populated municipality, had it not?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The municipality of Samac did not remain purely Serb. It is correct that --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I didn't say purely Serb. I said predominantly.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, predominantly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll turn to another topic. You mentioned in your evidence Crkvina, and you gave -- you said in evidence that in May of 1992 you learnt of a police operation whereby 100 to 150 people, Croats and Muslims, were taken to Crkvina for five or six days, and you said in evidence that you didn't know why they were taken there. Did you ever speculate back then, did you ever think that it might have something to do with their ethnicity, the fact that they were Croats and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The employees of the Red Cross, and I personally, were not involved in any kind of guesswork as to why somebody was taken away, but as the Red Cross, we tried to help these people. What the reasons were why they were taken away is something that I don't know, and I said that. We were primarily interested in the conditions under which these people lived and how we could help them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: That's right. But you and your activists had to go to Crkvina and work amongst these 100 to 150 Croat and Muslims, providing them with humanitarian care and so on. In the course of doing that, didn't one of them, any of them, explain to you why it was that they had been rounded up and taken to Crkvina, or were they all silent on the issue?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since this was a time of war, no explanation or clarification was given to the Red Cross about that. Our only task was to help people. As for the reasons why they were taken away, the employees of the Red Cross, and I personally, knew nothing about that. People who were there didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Forgetting about your role as director of social welfare, forgetting about the humanitarian intervention, what about normal human curiosity? What about just the fact that there was 100 to 150 people, fellow towns people, rounded up and taken there, just as a citizen, weren't you interested?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that we were not involved in any guesswork, and I cannot speculate now either.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: This operation of the rounding up and taking of people there was a drain on resources in Bosanski Samac, wasn't it, because of course you had to have the police involved, they had to round up the people, they had to guard the people, they had to transport the people. And the social work centre had to get involved, didn't it, by providing humanitarian aid. So it was quite a drain on the resources of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The workers of the Red Cross were informed one morning that there was a group of people there in the culture centre and that these people were in need of help. When they went there, they saw that these people were being guarded by the police. And the Red Cross activists could gain access and talk to them without any hindrance to see what kind of assistance they needed, and they did so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Yes, but -- thank you for telling us what happened. I'm not asking you what happened. What I'm asking you is another matter. The operation of rounding up these people, transporting them, guarding them, and providing humanitarian care was a drain on the precious resources of the municipality at that time, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the actual resources involved were, I don't know. I know about the engagement of the Red Cross, which involved the daily deliveries of food from Samac to this village, which is some five or six kilometres away. We didn't have to secure this humanitarian relief supplies; we just had to deliver it to the people in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: The operation would have drawn on the services of sufficient people for it to be a significant event in the administration of the municipality, wouldn't it? And as such, it would have been a matter that would have been of interest to the civilian authorities, Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness has explained repeatedly what he knew about -- knows about this operation and what his exact role was and what he knows about other organs. This repetition of the same question to which the witness has clearly replied. As far as his information and his knowledge about the factors concerned. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm not asking for endless repetition of what happened. I keep getting endless repetition of what happened. My inquiry is that the effect on the municipality of rounding up these people, the drain on resources, and whether or not such a matter would be known to the civilian administration, namely, these defendants, or two of these defendants. That's my area of interest. I keep getting a description of what happened, but it's not the description of what happened that I'm interested in; it's the effect of what happened that I'm interested in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. You can proceed. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Witness, I just want to -- I just want to establish a basic point. Rounding up 150 Croats and Muslims, using the police to do that and take them out to this place and keep them there for a week, that's a big drain on a war-torn, small municipality, and it's the sort of thing that must, of logic, have been known to the civilian administration, to the Crisis Staff; do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what had been known to the civilian administration who participated in these operations, but I know that when the Red Cross was informed of this incident, it was requested to help and exert every effort in order to help those people. I cannot say who participated in the operation and what the role of the civil authorities had been.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Well, I've taken that as far as I can go. I don't think I'm going to get any further, if Your Honours please, so I'll leave the topic. The status of these people was a matter of importance to you, wasn't it, that is, whether or not they were prisoners of war or criminals, or simply detainees engaged in some sort of local criminal act; would you agree?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, these were civilians, women and children and elderly people.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: That's right. And so it's unlikely, isn't it, that they were prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: It's unlikely that they had been arrested for insurrection or rebellion against the state or any other similar criminal act, treason or something like that?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I didn't know why they were there, and I cannot speculate about the reasons why they had been there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: These people were essentially prisoners, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were put up in the culture centre, and they were guarded by the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Taken from their homes, taken to somewhere else, guarded by the police, isn't that a prisoner? Wouldn't you agree?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly whether I would use the term "prisoner" or "detainees," but I know that it was not a prison. It was a culture centre in which they were held for a couple of days.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's not quibble about words. They were at least people who had undergone a loss of freedom; would you agree to that extent?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their freedom was certainly restricted by the very fact that they were being guarded by other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. If they had been --

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By the police, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: If they had been fully-fledged complete prisoners, that would be a matter of concern to the local Red Cross, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you report to the Executive Board or to the Crisis Staff on the events at Crkvina, the events that I've just been asking about, for example, to tell them how it was going, the humanitarian care?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We reported. We informed orally the Executive Board. And I believe that it was the result of our reporting to the Executive Board that these people were released and went home after a couple of days.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Right. Are you saying that you personally provided a report, or was it your agency? And how was that carried out? How did you do -- conduct the reporting?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Mihajlovic was the president of the Red Cross at that time, and he informed the Executive Board orally about the activities that the Red Cross had taken, undertaken vis-a-vis these people, about the conditions in which these people were living, the requests which they addressed to the Red Cross in terms of the required assistance, and about all the problems which -- with which they were afflicted, the diseases, the needs -- their need of medicaments and suchlike.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Tell me: Did Mr. Mihajlovic report to the Executive Board the reason why they had been arrested? Because, of course, if the Executive Board was going to do something intelligent about the situation, they had to know that, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether Mr. Mihajlovic talked about this particular issue with the members of the Executive Board, but I do know that when we had -- at a consultative meeting of the Red Cross, all these questions were addressed in detail, and that Mr. Mihajlovic informed the Executive Board about these issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: To whom in the Executive Board did he report? Who was made aware of the situation?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly which man among the members of the Executive Board was in charge of these issues at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure from your answer -- I understand that you don't know exactly which man, but are you suggesting that he reported to one man only or to a collection of men in the Executive Board?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The witness had said that Mr. Mihajlovic reported to the Executive Board. Is that not sufficient? I thought the Executive Board had certain responsibilities, from the evidence so far in the case. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. He did say that he doesn't know whether Mr. Mihajlovic talked about this particular issue with members of the board.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. It's when you asked him whether he -- whether Mr. Mihajlovic told the Executive Board the reasons why these people were held. That's when he answered like that. MR. DI FAZIO: Well, in any event, I've got as far as I want to go on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And can you recall when during this period of incarceration that the report was made?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that Mr. Mihajlovic informed the Executive Board about these issues on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Right. Thank you. So the Executive Board was kept updated by daily progress reports of the situation at Crkvina, the situation that we've been talking about?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: As far as you're aware, did this episode cause any fear or concern in the non-Serbian population of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot speak about the feelings of these people, but from my talking with them, they were quite upset and excited. But the very fact that they returned home, I believe changed their feelings. But of course these are their feelings, and I cannot speak about those.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. But I was actually asking you about the repercussions in the wider community. Did you detect any sense of fear or concern in the non-Serb population following this episode?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was fear, but this was characteristic of all the citizens in the municipality, and that was because of the war. So probably there was also fear in these citizens. What the repercussions were of this very episode on the citizens were, that is something I cannot say, because I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Following this episode, was there any sort of official explanation by the civilian authorities about why these 100 to 150 people, men, women, and children, had been rounded up and taken there?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Red Cross did not get any such explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And nor was one given to the wider community by the civilian authorities; correct?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Red Cross was not informed. Whether the wider community was informed, that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You also gave evidence in chief of the event at Crkvina where 15 to 16 people were murdered. You said that you heard about the event shortly thereafter. Did it become a matter of common knowledge in the town and in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This -- I learned about this event, this incident, when several people had been killed only later, and that was a very -- it was a very ugly and uncomfortable feeling for every person in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You say you only learnt about it later. In your evidence in chief, you said that you heard about it shortly thereafter. That was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I think in fairness to the witness, maybe it's a question of language. Shortly thereafter and later doesn't make much difference. MR. DI FAZIO: Okay. Perhaps it's not important. I just want to make sure that there's no resiling from the position that it was shortly thereafter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: When you said that you learnt about it shortly thereafter, what did you mean? How long after the event did you learn about it?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I heard this from the people there. There were stories. Actually, nobody wanted nor dared talk about these things because of the conduct of the person who had committed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I just remind you very briefly of the evidence you gave in chief on Friday, the 17th of January, page 15 of the LiveNote. You commented that the story was spread out throughout the town out of fear, that you couldn't hear this officially from anyone, that this was mentioned in talks in town, and there was fear among the people. That's what you said in evidence in chief in response to Mr. Lukic's questions. I take it from that that everybody knew what had happened at Crkvina.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said in my statement that I'd heard and that there were stories being spread out through town. But officially, I was never informed personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: I'm not asking about official -- your official -- being officially told of the episode. Just I want to hear -- what I want you to agree to, I'll be frank, is that the massacre was a matter of common knowledge throughout the town; everybody knew what had happened in that small warehouse at Crkvina.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say that everyone knew. As for the way in which I found out, actually, the way in which I found out indicates that quite a large number of people also knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And this is precisely the sort of issue that would cause unease and disquiet amongst the people, the non-Serbs, at least?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did the Red Cross do anything to allay the fears of the non-Serb population?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Will you please clarify this question? In what sense, fears?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: The fears that you -- the unease and disquiet that the people were feeling following the slaughter of 15 or 16 people. Did the Red Cross do anything to reassure the non-Serb population?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A large number of people, of citizens, came to the Red Cross every day, a large number of citizens of all ethnicities, requesting assistance in humanitarian issues. And as far as I know, the activists did not speak about these issues with anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did the Red Cross move to provide humanitarian care to the families of the victims, the people who had been killed at Crkvina?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Assistance was rendered, but the Red Cross in fact did not know who these people were at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Sorry. I don't get that. If you don't know who they are, how can you render assistance?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was speaking in general about rendition of assistance to people who came to the Red Cross, including people who were non-Serbs. And I'm talking about humanitarian assistance: Food, clothing, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Yes, but I wasn't speaking in general, I was speaking in specific. I'm asking you: Was assistance rendered to the families of the people killed at Crkvina by the centre of social welfare or the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say specifically what assistance was rendered to those people, because the Red Cross didn't know who those people were.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Following this murder at Crkvina, it was clear, wasn't it, that the plight of prisoners was really far more severe than not very good food or not very good conditions or beatings and they were actually being slaughtered? Did you speak to the ICRC about this and try and enlist their aid in doing something about it?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We spoke to them with the delegates of the ICRC, that is, about all the conditions in which these people were living, we informed them about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: No. I mean, did you speak to them about the deaths at Crkvina of the people who had been in custody?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In contact with them, and I mean the activists of the ICRC, we told them that we had heard, and the delegate of the International Red Cross said that he also had information about such an incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Intervention in respect of the translation. Line 12, page 20. The witness said in contact with them, and I mean the activists of the -- oh, he meant the activists of the -- he said "we, the activists of the Red Cross informed them." This is not what the translation, what the transcript says. So please can this be clarified. That's page 21.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. Clarify that with the witness. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You spoke to the ICRC, that is, your local Red Cross activists spoke to the ICRC about the deaths that had taken place at Crkvina; correct?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and we told them how we had learned about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you provide any information as to who had committed the murders, for example, that it was Lugar?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We could not provide them with a name, because there were stories being bandied about. There was no official information. The delegate of the Red Cross told us that he would talk to the representatives of the police about this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me. Mr. Maslic, which delegate of the ICRC was the communication made with? Is it one of the two persons that we've heard about already in your testimony, the lady, Ms. Katherine, or Mr. Matteas? Or was it somebody different? It would be, I think, important for us to know who the communication was made with.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Katherine was there at the very beginning, and she soon left the area. And after her, Mr. Matteas was there, and we talked to Mr. Matteas about this. He was with an interpreter. He had an interpreter throughout his period, and I believe that he remained in the area with his office in Bijeljina throughout 1992 and 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: And one follow-up question: Do you know whether Mr. Matteas relayed this information back to ICRC headquarters in Geneva and whether any steps were taken by the ICRC?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not know whether he relayed this information to them. I know that he always joined in in all of these activities. And as to the way in which he transmitted information to his superiors, I don't know about that, because he never informed us about how he did that, nor was he under any obligation to. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You've already testified that this issue, this event at Crkvina, had caused fear in the -- or concern in the Croat and Muslim population. As a result of that, did you consider, or did you in fact discuss the consequences with leading figures in the civilian administration? By that I mean people like Blagoje Simic or Mirko Lukic or Simeon Simic or Bozo Ninkovic or Stevan Todorovic.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've said that I myself have had trouble with that man. There was fear among all the citizens regarding this kind of behaviour and what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Which man did you say that you had had trouble with?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lugar. Lugar. I said that in response to Mr. Lukic's question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. But did you speak to those people whom I've mentioned, Blagoje Simic, about the consequences of the murders in the non-Serb community?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that Mr. Mihajlovic was president at the time, and he was the one who contacted the Executive Board. I never discussed the subject with Mr. Simic, or other issues either, because we only had a line of contact with the Executive Board. As for contacts with the Executive Board, Mr. Lukic had also heard about this event.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Mirko Lukic?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Do you know if Mr. Mihajlovic told Blagoje Simic about the concerns?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I know that the Executive Board was informed, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did you ever speak informally with any of these people, the people whose names I've mentioned, regarding the consequences of these murders at Crkvina?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't discuss it with anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You testified that in the summer of 1992, police took Croats and Muslims to Zasavica, and you don't know why. You testified that Zasavica had police guards and that entry in and out was controlled by the police. Do you recall that evidence?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Those people were, in effect, detained there, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not a prison, but their movement was restricted within that village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: They were prisoners there. They might not have had bars, but they were prisoners. They couldn't move in and out, their freedom had been curtailed; right?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They could not leave the village because there was a police checkpoint there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Now, Matteas was the man who asked to go to Zasavica. It was not your idea, was it?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Red Cross activists went to Zasavica immediately, as soon as they heard that people had been taken there. This was at the request of Mr. Ivica Pandurevic, who was commissioner of that village. He came to the Red Cross and asked that assistance be increased, in view of the increase in the population of that village then. When Mr. Matteas came to Samac for the first time and asked about Zasavica, the activists told him about what the situation was like there. He asked for someone to go there with him, and he said that previously he had received approval from the police to go there. I agreed to accompany him personally to Zasavica, so I went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You did not engineer or make any moves to take Mr. Matteas to see these non-Serbs whose freedom had been curtailed. You did not arrange that. It was him -- it was Mr. Matteas who came to you?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said that Red Cross activists, as soon as they found out about the fact that people were taken to Zasavica, that is, went to the Red Cross and measures were taken. Matteas came soon, and that is when I personally took part in this. I did not go before that because it was Red Cross activists who had gone. On the basis of their reports, the oral reports they made, one could see that the situation there and the living conditions of the citizens there were not that bad but that assistance should be given and that this assistance should be increased, should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You said that as soon as they found out that people had been taken to Zasavica, the activists went to the Red Cross and measures were taken. Do you mean the local Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said activists of the local Red Cross went to Zasavica, not the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. But the measures that were taken were entirely at the initiative of the local Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: When you took Matteas to Zasavica, did he show any interest in the reason for the detention of these Croats at Zasavica or for the isolation or the curtailment of the freedom, whatever expression you want to give it?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Matteas showed great interest in that village. When entering the village, he passed through the entire village in his vehicle. Then we went to Mr. Pandurevic the commissioner for that village and we talked to him. Mr. Matteas asked me to make it possible for him to talk individually to each and every inhabitant of that village in order to become aware of the living conditions of people in that village. I stayed with Mr. Pandurevic in a house, and he talked to people in the village. He stayed for quite a while then. He talked about the reasons --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Sorry. You were going to say he talked about some reasons. What reasons?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reasons why people were brought in, also their demands, the ones they addressed to the International Committee of the Red Cross. He did not talk about that to me. However, when returning from Zasavica, when he returned to the office of the local Red Cross, we agreed what was needed, and on the basis of that we sent a request to the Executive Board of the Municipal Assembly for additional assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Look, we're just getting a description of what happened, and I'm not interested in precisely a step-by-step description of what happened. My question is simply this: The reason for people to have been taken to Zasavica. Now, you said that he talked about the reasons why people were brought in. What reasons were they? Why were people brought in to Zasavica?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that he talked to the local people in Zasavica. And then what did he talk about? I said about the reasons and about their demands, about their living conditions, and all questions -- I mean, he did not inform me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But when coming to the local Red Cross --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the entire problem is due to a mistake in the transcript. Page 26, line 15, the witness started the -- started saying the reasons, and it says here he talked about the reasons. I think that that is what is confusing the witness. The tape can be heard, in that sentence. Line 15, he said: "About the reasons --" perhaps it is this particular translation that is causing confusion, so perhaps we should avoid confusion. MR. DI FAZIO: I'd be grateful to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Let me ask you this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Di Fazio. Just one question for Mr. Maslic. Mr. Maslic, we've heard in testimony here before the Trial Chamber that some of the families whose men, brothers, sons, fathers, had left Bosanski Samac and swum across the River Sava to Croatia, that the families of these persons were taken to Zasavica. Are you aware of that at all? Did you hear anything in town about that or from some other source?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard that there were departures from the territory of the municipality of Samac before the war conflict broke out, and I heard that a group swam across the Sava. I don't know how many people were involved and who these people were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: And -- well, the second part of the question was: Did you hear that the -- you know, the mothers, wives, sisters of such men who had swum across the River Sava were collected and taken to live in Zasavica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether it was only those families of those persons, and I don't know who these persons were, so in that group I don't know who are the persons who were taken away. Was it these families or somebody else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: So is that a yes or a no? You don't know? You don't know? Or is it --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You are not aware of connection of men swimming across the Sava River to Croatia and the taking of Croats to Zasavica? The two events are unconnected, as far as you're aware?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of the reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's get back to the visit of Mr. Matteas to Zasavica. At any time during your visit to Zasavica, did you hear anyone explain to Mr. Matteas the reason for their being there, any of the Croats who had been taken there?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that Mr. Matteas, when talking to these citizens, asked that the representatives of the local Red Cross should not be present. I don't know what kind of information he received from citizens who were in Zasavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, did Mr. Matteas seek directly from you, did he ever ask you: Mr. Maslic, what is the reason for these Croats to be here in Zasavica? And if he did ask you, did you give an answer?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not ask the local Red Cross that. He was aware of the jurisdiction of the police and of the role of the Red Cross. So he did not ask us about the reasons, and we did not know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: You keep saying us and we. I assume, therefore, that he did not ask you personally.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to the local Red Cross and its activists.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did he ask you personally, did he ask you, Velimir Maslic: What is the reason for these Croats to be here in Zasavica?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he did not ask me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: This situation was unusual, wasn't it? It was not usual for most of the population to be rounded up and taken to a particular village?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's unusual, but there were quite a few unusual things taking place regarding movements of the population within the war zone itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Yes. No doubt. And furthermore, the ICRC were interested in the events at Zasavica that we've been talking about. Did the unusual nature of the event, plus the ICRC interest, cause you to report to the civilian authorities on what was going on at Zasavica and on your visit with the ICRC there?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not the only reason. There were several reasons there. This is a village with an express need for help and with an expressed desire and willingness on the part of the delegate of the International Red Cross in respect of that village. Our duty is to take part, to give assistance, and to inform about activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not asking you about your duties. All I'm asking you is this: It was a slightly -- an unusual situation, with Croats being specifically taken to this one village, and furthermore, the ICRC are interested and they're asking to go and visit the village. This was a situation that called for a report to the civilian authorities, wasn't it, a report by you to the civilian authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his answer? The interpreters could not understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can the witness repeat the whole answer? The interpreters said they didn't catch it. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Yes. Could you -- you weren't recorded -- we couldn't hear what you said, so could you just give us your answer once again, please, what you just said.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yes, and that was not the only reason why we informed the civilian structures of authority. Because the gentleman from the International Red Cross had come earlier too. His visit was one of the many regular visits he paid to our municipality and to other local communes in addition to Zasavica. It is a fact that there was multi-fold interest in Zasavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Right. And so did you -- you provided this report and you said to the civilian authorities: Let's go through in more detail the persons to whom you reported. Firstly, did you report to the Executive Board and the Crisis Staff, or was it only just the Executive Board?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Executive Board was informed about that. It was informed about all measures and activities of the local Red Cross and the International Red Cross. We particularly pointed out that it was necessary to give special emphasis to the local clinic in that village, because citizens could not leave that village of their own free will. So then that was done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Your time is coming to a close, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I've got this topic to finish, which I've just about finished. I've not got very much more. And I've then got one last remaining topic, which is -- and that's it. I don't think I'll be able to finish -- obviously, I won't be able to finish before 10.30, and I'll probably need about half an hour thereafter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. Mr. Di Fazio. Yesterday I told you, you had one hour. This morning it's been extended one and a half hours. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. Well, I understood yesterday that we would approach the issue of how long I had this morning, depending on the circumstances. I can tell Your Honours what I have to do, what I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So you go ahead and when we come back you have 15 minutes to wind up. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Did the Executive Board -- sorry. In the course of your reporting to the Executive Board about events in Zasavica, you told them, they were obviously aware, weren't they, of the fact that it was Croats who had been taken to Zasavica?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Croats and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And did the Executive Board report on that to the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness did respond, but I would like to ask the Prosecutor, because of my entire line of questioning: When he speaks about the Crisis Staff, he should refer only to the period up to July, and after July, it is the War Presidency. And all these events took place after the Crisis Staff ceased to exist. And the Trial Chamber is aware of this. So I don't really object, but as regards future questions that would be put by the Prosecutor, could he please bear in mind the fact that after July the right term to be used is the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the interpreters please ask Mr. Lukic to slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Sorry. Would Your Honours just bear with me for one moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: In the course of providing those reports to the Executive Board, it was made clear, wasn't it, that the Croats were being detained there, that is, they couldn't leave?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've already said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. And just before the break, we'll move on to one further question. Did the Executive Board in turn report to the War Presidency regarding the detention of these Croats at Zasavica?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Did you ever speak to Blagoje Simic about the Croats at Zasavica?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have any contacts with Blagoje Simic, and I didn't inform him about anything, because we had an Executive Board, a body that we were duty-bound to report to.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And can you tell us who in particular, which man in particular, you told of the situation at Zasavica and the detained Croats?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said the Executive Board, and I am referring to a body.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: But you can't remember which men specifically? It doesn't matter that much, but if you can remember, tell us.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, if we break now, it's only 10.29, I'll have an opportunity to go through my notes and tailor it a bit more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well. We shall take our break now and continue at 1100 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Mr. Maslic, you recall your evidence both in examination-in-chief and cross-examination that the International Committee of the Red Cross played a leading role in the organisation of the first exchange, at least. Do you recall that evidence?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And is it your position that other international organisations, including the United Nations, assisted in that process, United Nations agencies?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The International Red Cross participated in the exchanges, rendered assistance, and on such occasions, also at the request of the opposite side, at the request of our side, as well as of the citizens they provided assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. But as far as international organisations are concerned, do you limit your evidence to the ICRC? That was the only international organisation that you observed facilitating the process of exchange?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In addition to the Red Cross, other organisations would also be involved, humanitarian organisations, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Right. International --

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depending on --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. All I want to know: These other organisations, are they international humanitarian organisations?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was about to say that depending on the actual terms of reference of the organisation in question, for instance, the UNHCR assisted the population a great deal in food, in getting them in touch with their separate families.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. But I'm interested specifically in the exchanges. As far as the exchanges are concerned, you've already testified that the ICRC played a leading role in organising and facilitating these exchanges which you've described to the Chamber. In addition to the ICRC, did other international humanitarian organisations facilitate and participate in the exchange processes that you have described? Did you see that taking place?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, other humanitarian organisations did not participate in any exchanges. I said that the United Nations forces provided assistance in terms of security, of securing the place where the negotiations and the exchanges were taking place. I've already described that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I understand your position. Mr. Maslic, the UN commission on human rights provided a report on the situation of human rights in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, and that was submitted by the Special Rapporteur, Mr. Tadeusz, T-A-D-E-U-S-Z, Mazowiecki, M-A-Z-O-W-I-E-C-K-I. Mr. Tadeusz Mazowiecki, a Special Rapporteur, and he provided his first report on the 28th of August, 1992, after a visit to the area of the former Yugoslavia, and in particular, Bosnia, between the 21st and the 26th of August, 1992. Part of his report is section D, and he deals there with the difficulties affecting the functioning of humanitarian organisations. And I want to read to you paragraph 50 of that report and obtain your comment, please. Paragraph 50: "In territories --"

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we should first ask the witness whether he's aware of that report at all, and then to see how the question should be phrased for a comment on his part. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, we have a B/C/S version of the particular paragraph. It's not an official translation, but as a tool, it might be useful for the witness so he can follow the content of the paragraph that I wish to read to him. If there's no objection, I'll provide it to him. I wouldn't seek to tender it. It's not an official translation, but it's a tool.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, but the document you're dealing with, it's a UN document, isn't it. MR. DI FAZIO: It's a UN document in English. Do you wish me to give him this draft translation of the particular paragraph that I want to show him or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. I thought that if you read the interpreters will follow, as long as you read slowly. Because you are calling that other thing a draft translation. The Trial Chamber isn't sure. MR. DI FAZIO: Fine. I'll read out the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic's objection was that he wanted you to find out from the witness whether he had ever heard of the report. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Have you heard of this report that I'm referring to? Do you know of it?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I haven't. I'm not aware of this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I cannot comment on it, not being aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Certainly. Okay. But you can comment on some of the observations of the Special Rapporteur, since you were there on the ground. Now, let me read the paragraph to you, and I'll ask you some questions about it: "In territories of Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina under the control of ethnic Serbs, international organisations have repeatedly encountered special difficulties in deciding whether or not they should compromise their principles in order to avoid tragic loss of life. The forces responsible for carrying out ethnic cleansing deliberately put such humanitarian bodies in the position of either becoming reluctant accomplices to ethnic cleansing by helping move target groups out of the area being cleansed to an area of safety under the control of other parties, or leaving them to their fate, which according to the circumstances, may be detention, starvation, or the risk of summary execution." Do you agree with that assessment?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot agree with this assessment, from my standpoint. I'm no expert. To interpret this kind of a subject-matter. But I can say that the International Red Cross, as a humanitarian organisation, as well as its delegates who had their mandates, themselves exhibited an interest and a desire to help the people that found itself in the war-ridden areas and to provide them with every kind of assistance, including also the crossing over to the other side to respect the principle of the reunification of families.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And certainly from what you saw and observed of the exchanges in the area of Bosanski Samac, the ICRC was anything but a reluctant accomplice, on the contrary; it was playing a leading role in the exchanges?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the International Red Cross was not a reluctant accomplice, collaborator, but what I said was that the International Red Cross exhibited great interest, was really bent on, keen, to help the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I seek to tender that report into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I thought we took judicial notice of UN documents. It's a public one, isn't it? Unless you want specifically that paragraph. MR. DI FAZIO: Well, yes. Yes, I do want specifically that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. There's no harm, then. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. And if Your Honours please, just while that's being done, I can wrap up my questioning, if I may just proceed with another question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Can we have the number, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit P161. Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Mr. Maslic, I suggest to you that your evidence regarding the ICRC brokering, organising, facilitating the exchange and the exchanges that you've talked about is untrue, that they did not play that sort of role in the organisation of the exchanges. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And I put it to you that the exchanges that you have described were in fact a thinly veiled disguise over a crisis of ethnic cleansing that was going on in the municipality of Bosanski Samac. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: And I put it to you that that policy was largely successful, the end result being that large numbers of non-Serbs had driven out of the municipality via the system of exchanges. Do you agree or disagree?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that nobody had been driven out, and I've said during my testimony that citizens reported of their own free will, of their own initiative, and reported their desires to cross over to the other side. Also, citizens from the other side who wished to cross over to the territory of our municipality acted in a similar fashion.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI
utterances.text: Thank you very much. MR. DI FAZIO: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Re-examination, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. Will document 146/42 be shown to the witness, please, again, for just a brief while, that is, P146/42. Mr. Maslic, yesterday the Prosecutor showed you this document and asked you if the Muslim commission made any distinction between detained persons and civilians, and asked you to take a look at the title of the commission and the title was "Commission for the exchange and flow of civilians." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Will you please read the title for me of this document slowly.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "List of persons-civilians who are being sought to be exchanged from the area of Samac-Modrica and the general area, to the area of Lukavac and the general area."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Does the title of this document -- is it -- according to the title of this document, is this a free circulation of citizens in question or are they being sought to be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are being sought to be exchanged, because that was the only way that such a crossing could have been made.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said to the Prosecutor, in response to his question, that -- yesterday, that Mr. Matteas, after having talked to you, went to the SUP, the secretariat of the interior, and told you what he had seen. Do you know that before he went to report to the police, did he go and actually see for himself these detainees?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure when it was that he exactly went there. I know that he did go to visit the detention units. He was interested in the people who were being held there. And his contacts with the police in respect of his visits to these places and the interviews -- and the talks after that is what he had with the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Maslic, did Mr. Matteas take his own personal interpreter with him when he went to do these interviews, or was an interpreter supplied by the police? If you know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that Mr. Matteas had an interpreter. Her name was Snezana, Mrs. Snezana, I believe, and he always had an interpreter with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. I realise that you said he had an interpreter. My question was: Do you know whether she was the one or the personal interpreter was the one who went with him when he interviewed the detainees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know how he went and how he talked to the detainees, because we didn't go there. We couldn't go there when he went there, I mean the activists of the Red Cross. I can only suppose that that was so, because he would never have any talks without an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Matteas, since he started coming, and you explained to me and the Prosecutor that he came there -- went there quite frequently, did he ever say to either you in person or your colleagues and you heard that any of the colleagues who had come previously, I mean Katherine, had raised any objections vis-a-vis your work and the first exchange? So had any of his colleagues have any complaints about that first exchange and your work in connection with it?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never heard Mr. Matteas convey any objections to the work of the local Red Cross in respect of the previous work of the delegates of the Red Cross and as regards his work and his cooperation with the local Red Cross, he always spoke about it in favourable terms when we had meetings, and he always had some remarks in the sense of what else needed to be done, and he always had more and more requirements in that sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You didn't fully respond to my question. You said that he didn't have objections to the work the local Red Cross, but what I asked you was whether he had any -- he had heard any objections having been raised by his colleagues to the first exchange in Zasavica.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't say that he had heard any such objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor asked you yesterday about persons who went to the line to state their opinions, their preferred options, to the opposite side in the sense they were not willing to cross. Was there not a much more appropriate way for that to be done in Samac, in view of the dangers that entailed? My question is: Do you know that a single person that you, your commission, the Exchange Commission, of these persons who you took to the line to either state their views or actually state their options, was any of these individuals ever hurt or suffered in any way, God forbid?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, no one of these persons came to any harm, and to the best of my knowledge, they moved about freely and lived in the houses in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm asking during the actual process of exchange, did anyone come to any harm?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did any person go missing during the actual exchange?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, responding to a question by the Prosecutor, you said that people stated their preferred options before the representatives of the International Red Cross when they were present at the exchange. Was it irrespective of whether the International Red Cross was absent or present at the exchange, was it always the case that these people always stated their views to the opposite side?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you have situations of a person being sought repeatedly, many times, to come and state his preferred option again?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was it their families who were in fact insisting to hear from their relatives directly whether they wished to cross or not?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were such instances, and in such instances we made it possible for their families to come there to the spot and to see their people at the separation line and to talk to each other freely, in order to agree what it is that they actually wanted in terms of being sought or their remaining in Samac. As far as I know, there were several such families. They are still living in Samac and they did not cross over to the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The Honourable Judge Williams asked you, and the Prosecutor also followed up on that question in respect of Article 143 of the Geneva Convention regarding visits to the -- to people in prison. My question is: Are you familiar with the Geneva Conventions?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have read the Geneva Convention. I had occasion to familiarise myself with it. But I'm not versed in every detail. Of course, it needs closer scrutiny as a document. But I have read it in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: While you worked at these exchanges, did you bear in mind Article 26 of the Geneva Convention, of the 4th Geneva Convention? I shall quote it for you: "Every party to the conflict shall facilitate research undertaken by members of the families that have been broken up by the war in order for them to be re-established ties, mutual ties, and to meet again if that is possible. It will, in particular, facilitate the work of organisations dedicated to this task on condition that they have recognised these organisations and that they adapt their work to the security measures undertaken by that side." MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I object to the question. Firstly, it's cross-examining the witness, and not only that, but it's also placing the answer clearly in his mouth. The purpose of re-examination is to clarify anything that arose in the course of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I thought this arose in the course of cross-examination. MR. DI FAZIO: Not the specifics of the convention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: There's nothing wrong. I mean, the Geneva Conventions arose during cross-examination, so Mr. Lukic is in order.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know about this particular article? Did it ever mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of this article of the convention. As for these activities that were carried out within the Red Cross, they were related precisely to that article and its implementation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The Prosecutor asked you today about your membership in the SDS. I'm going to put a brief question to you. Were people free to join the SDS in 1993, 1994, and 1995?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was possible to join freely. Everybody acted according to his own free will and his or her wish to join a political party.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But at that time you didn't?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time I didn't want to join a single political party, because of the war itself and because of the circumstances under which we worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor asked you about the regulations that were implemented in the work of your centre and of the local Red Cross. You already explained that to the Prosecutor, but I would seek further clarification. The laws that you mentioned during my examination-in-chief as well, when were these laws actually adopted, the ones that you applied while you worked at the centre and at the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke about regulations from the field of social welfare and child care. These are regulations that were passed before the war in the former Bosnia-Herzegovina, and they were being applied at the time while I was director of the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor asked you today whether the municipality, due to exchanges, had become predominantly Serb populated. I'm going to ask you whether people left the municipality of Samac in other ways, not only by way of exchanges.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
