utterances.text: They left by way of going to Yugoslavia, to Serbia. Whether there was any other way in which this territory was left, I cannot say. However, my family was also in Yugoslavia as refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the -- do you know whether most of the population left by way of exchanges or some other way? I'm referring to the non-Serb population.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They left in other ways too, and the municipality was divided during the war. So a significant part of populated areas remained in the Federation, that is to say, BH, with a predominantly different kind of population, like Domaljevac, Grebnice, Bazik.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That was not my question. Since you worked on exchanges, can you say whether the non-Serb population that had left the territory of the municipality of Samac left through exchanges for the most part or in some other way?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of them left in some other way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. Maslic, can we find out, though, in response to Mr. Lukic's question: These other ways, could you elaborate a little bit? In which other ways did people leave the non-Serb population, apart from the exchanges?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During the first days of the war, of the war conflict, citizens could leave the territory of the municipality. During those first few days of the war, they could leave and they did leave from the territory of the municipality. When a line of fire was established, such departures were not possible. One could only go to Serbia, to Yugoslavia, and to Croatia in this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: We've heard that checkpoints were set up around the town of Bosanski Samac and that passes had to be issued by Mr. Todorovic and the military, depending on who the people were. This seems to imply that there wasn't total freedom of movement. Would you be able to again just elaborate very briefly, you know? Is my understanding, from what we've heard to date correct, that there were checkpoints and people had to have passes in order to be able to move in and out of town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Later they had to. At the very beginning of my testimony, I said that I, together with my family, was outside the municipality during the first days of the war. A great many families, during the first days of the war and on the eve of the war itself temporarily moved out of the municipality because this conflict was being felt, and also the closeness of the war in Croatia. During these first few days of the war, most people from the municipality of Samac, of all ethnic backgrounds, had left in order to avoid these clashes and deaths. Later, when checkpoints were established, the movement of the population was under control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, and for the purposes of assisting you, we should have this witness's position absolutely clear, now that Mr. Lukic has raised this issue in re-examination. The witness said that most people left by way other than the exchanges, by other mechanisms, and that occurred in the first few days of the war. You should know, I submit, whether this witness's position is that most of the non-Serbs who left the municipality of Bosanski Samac did so at the very beginning, in the first few days of the war, or whether it was via the exchanges. Because it's not entirely clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Restricting the people who left to the non-Serb community. MR. DI FAZIO: I understand his position is most of the non-Serbs left in the initial, first few days of the war by some means other than exchanges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: And so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You just want that clarified. MR. DI FAZIO: The proportionality has to be clear, whether or not the subsequent exchange process got rid of - sorry - resulted in more non-Serbs leaving than the initial outflow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic. Clarify that with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you understand? Did you understand what the Prosecutor is insisting upon? Could you explain your views, your knowledge about the facts in relation to the non-Serb population that lived in the territory of the municipality of Samac that had left the territory of the municipality of Samac? Not those that you mentioned who stayed in Domaljevac, et cetera. So out of those who left, most of these people, did they leave before the war or as soon as the war broke out, or did most of that population remain in Samac and did they go elsewhere during the war, by way of exchanges or in other ways? I think that that was the gist of the Prosecutor's question.

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They left before the war started and during the first few days of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that we've clarified this, haven't we, as far as the Prosecutor is concerned? MR. DI FAZIO: We've clarified it as far as the witness is concerned, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what the Prosecutor wanted to hear from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maslic, do you know that during the first few days of the war, immediately after the 17th of April, about 3.500 inhabitants from Croat villages in the territory of the municipality of Samac had left? I'm referring to Novo Selo, Tisina, and these villages, Hasici, those who were in that part of the municipality of Samac. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I object to that question. It's raising an entirely new topic, one that was not raised in the cross-examination, and furthermore has the added problem of it being a highly leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic. That wasn't raised in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll give up on this question altogether, but I think that this question is derived from what Mr. Di Fazio asked in relation to exchanges and leaving the territory altogether during his cross-examination. But I'll leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Have you heard of Mr. Mirko Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've heard of him. As far as I can remember, he was president of the Executive Board just before the war broke out.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that he was president of the Executive Board in May 1992? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly how long, until when he was president of the Executive Board, but I know that he was president of the Executive Board just before the war and when the war began.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You also talked today about what you knew concerning the massacre in Crkvina, and also about Lugar and about the rumours and about what people said concerning that event. The Prosecutor asked you whether you had the impression that the non-Serb population became fearful after learning about this event. My question to you is whether you personally, as a person, and your co-workers at the Red Cross, did you become fearful of this man after having heard about this event?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This fear did exist. I was personally afraid of that man. And during my testimony, I said that he had threatened me. So there was fear.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm going to put another question to you related to this UN report that the Prosecutor read out, and also in relation to your cooperation with the International Red Cross. Mr. Maslic, have you heard of the name of Cornelio Sommaruga?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have. That was the president of the International Committee of the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the International Red Cross issued public statements, press releases, in 1992 and 1993, concerning their work in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about that, but I did not have an opportunity of reading these press releases or statements, so I'm not aware of their contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As the Prosecutor showed you a document and read a document to you a while ago, I'm now going to read another document to you and ask you for your comment. This is a statement for the public by Mr. Cornelio Sommaruga dated the 3rd of October, 1992. This is a document that we -- MR. DI FAZIO: May I please see the document? I haven't received it. May I see it before any further questions are asked on the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document was disclosed to the Prosecution in 2001, and the Prosecution has it under document -- under number PDB 56/3. This is a document that we said we would be exhibiting. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. And might I just have an opportunity to look at the document first, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. Before any further questions arise on the issue, if I might just ask for a moment to look at the document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have copies ready for the Trial Chamber, so could I please ask the usher. The document is in the English language. I haven't got the B/C/S version with me. I'm only interested in two sentences from this document.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters ask that the document be placed on the ELMO, please, as we have not received any copies. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. We've got no problem with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic. You can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Maslic, let us provide copies to the interpreters now as well. I'm going to read page 3 of this document. I'm going to read this slowly. I'll be reading in the English language. [In English] "In practical terms, this means that the parties involved, if necessary with help of the international protection forces, must take all necessary measures to: "1. Ensure that humanitarian organisation have unrestricted access to all civilian victims of the conflict, so that they can be protected and assisted in their places of the residence." [Interpretation] I'm interested in your comment with regard to the following two articles. [In English] "2. Facilitate the transfer of the most vulnerable civilians and those wishing to be reunited with their families and allow them to reach safe areas. "3. Arrange, as stipulated in the London agreements, for the unconditional release of all prisoners, who should also be permitted to join their families and resettle in safe areas or another country until they can return to their homes." [Interpretation] Mr. Maslic, during your work concerning exchanges, did you make an effort to abide by these positions of the International Red Cross and the statements made by its president?

utterances.speaker: VELIMIR MASLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During my testimony, on several occasions I pointed out the good cooperation we had with the International Committee of the Red Cross and the assistance we got, and also the major efforts and sacrifices made by its delegates, in order to go along with the wishes and willingness of those who were afflicted by war. We were primarily guided by the principle of family reunification, so that people would be saved rather than become victims of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have an exhibit number for this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit D104/3.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that completes my re-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Maslic, for giving evidence to the Trial Chamber. You are now finished. You may leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to thank Your Honours for giving me this opportunity to take the witness stand in front of this Tribunal. I hope that my testimony will help you in performing your duties. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. It will be very helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, before we call the next witness, we would like to propose some measures in respect of this witness in private session. So if we can now proceed in private session for our explanation of why we seek these measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Can we go into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The next witness will give evidence in closed session, upon the request of the Defence. There is no objection from the Prosecution, and the Trial Chamber is of the view that in the interests of justice, it's better to hear this witness in closed session.
